claim: β-catenin is highly conserved across metazoan, with a central armadillo repeat domain consisting of twelve repeats.
source: β-cat is highly conserved across metazoan, with a central armadillo repeat domain consisting of twelve repeats (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 1a showing the structure.

claim: The twelve armadillo repeats form a spring-like superhelix featuring a long, positively charged groove that interacts with several key residues of the cytoplasmic tail of E-cadherin.
source: These repeats form a spring like superhelix featuring a long, positively charged groove that interacts with several key residues of the cytoplasmic tail of E-cad (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a) (Huber and Weis, 2001; Orsulic and Peifer, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior structural studies and referenced figure.

claim: Phosphorylation of β-catenin on tyrosine Y654 reduces the affinity of E-cadherin to β-catenin by approximately 86%.
source: The strength of interaction is dynamically modulated, mostly by the phosphorylation of β-cat on tyrosine Y654 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b,c in red), reducing the affinity of E-cad to β-cat by approximately 86% (Roura et al., 1999; van Veelen et al., 2011).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to prior experimental work.

claim: In mammalian cells, phosphorylation of β-catenin Y654 involves Src-family kinases.
source: In mammalian cells, phosphorylation of β-cat Y654 has been shown to involve SFK (Roura et al., 1999).
evidence: Stated with citation to prior research.

claim: The Drosophila Armadillo Y667 site shows sequence similarity to the conserved Src-phosphorylation site at Y654 in mouse.
source: In Drosophila, the Y667 site of the β-cat homologue Armadillo shows sequence similarity to the conserved Src-phosphorylation site at Y654 in mouse (Brunet et al., 2013; Roura et al., 1999; van Veelen et al., 2011) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Stated with citations and supported by sequence alignment figure.

claim: The Drosophila E-cadherin D1170 interacting site shows sequence conservation with the D665 mouse site.
source: Its Drosophila E-cad D1170 interacting site similarly shows sequence conservation with the D665 mice site (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e) (Huber and Weis, 2001).
evidence: Stated with citation and supported by sequence alignment figure.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations were performed on the β-catenin-E-cadherin complex submitted to a stretching uniaxial force.
source: To test the hypothesis of a mechanical opening of the Y654-β-cat/E-cad-D665 site as the primary mechantransductive molecular event initiating the mechanical activation of the β-cat pathway, and gain insight at the molecular level, we performed molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of the β-cat-E-cad complex submitted to a stretching uniaxial force (Huang and MacKerell, 2013; Phillips et al., 2005).
evidence: Directly stated as a method used in the study.

claim: The force in the simulations is applied on E-cadherin by both the cell's and the neighbouring cell's apical constrictions that drive Drosophila embryo mesoderm invagination.
source: The force is applied on E-Cad by both the cell's and the neighbouring cell's apical constrictions that drive Drosophila embryos mesoderm invagination (Sweeton et al., 1991).
evidence: Stated with citation to prior work on mesoderm invagination.

claim: The force acts perpendicular to the plasma membrane directed to the outside, with β-catenin fixed at its Y142 interacting site with α-catenin which is connected to the actin cytoskeleton.
source: It thus acts perpendicular to the plasma membrane directed to the outside, with β-cat fixed at its Y142 interacting site with α-catenin which is connected to the Actin cytoskeleton (Xu and Kimelman, 2007) (Figure 1a).
evidence: Stated with citation and illustrated in figure.

claim: Conventional MD simulations are limited to timescales of hundreds of nanoseconds to the microsecond.
source: Note that the timescales of conventional MD simulations are currently limited to the hundreds of nanoseconds to the microsecond.
evidence: Statement about technical limitations of MD simulations.

claim: To observe protein unfolding or conformational changes in response to mechanical force on reduced timescales, it is common to use forces that are higher than experimental ones.
source: To observe protein unfolding, or conformational changes in response to mechanical force on such a reduced timescale, it is therefore common to use forces that are higher than experimental ones.
evidence: Statement about standard practice in MD simulations.

claim: Twenty independent simulations were generated for a total simulation time of 30 ns each (600 ns total) on a protein complex of more than 500 residues.
source: Here, we generated 20 independent simulations for a total simulation time of 30 ns each (600 ns total) on a protein complex of significant size (more than 500 residues).
evidence: Directly stated as the simulation parameters used.

claim: The simulations under strain employed a constant force of 150 pN to observe relevant conformational changes on the 30-ns timescale.
source: Our simulations under strain employed a constant force of 150 pN in order to observe relevant conformational changes on the 30-ns timescale of the simulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Directly stated as the simulation parameter.

claim: The mean elongation of the simulated complex showing the opening of the Y654-D665 site on the timescale of 12 ns is 6 nm.
source: The mean elongation of the simulated complex showing the opening of the Y654-D665 site on the timescale of 12 ns is of 6 nm (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Directly stated as a result from the simulations.

claim: The modulus of elasticity of an α-helix is on the order of 1 pN/nm.
source: The proteins including β-cat are formed by α-helices only, with a modulus of elasticity of Kh of an α-helix on the order of 1 pN/nm (Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated with citation to prior work.

claim: The 6 nm elongation corresponds to a force of 6 pN, consistent with the 2-3 pN characteristic force of E-cadherin in adherent cells without external force.
source: Therefore we find that this elongation corresponds to a force of 6 pN, consistent with the 2-3 pN characteristic force of E-cad in adherent cells without external force (Borghi et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated as a calculation result with citation to prior work for comparison.

claim: After a global extension of 8 nm of the overall complex, a local stretching deformation of 1.25 ± 0.6 nm (45% strain) is observed between the A648 site of the α-helix HII-E-cadherin and the C-terminus of the α-helix H3-β-catenin.
source: After a global extension of 8 nm of the overall complex, a local and fine stretching deformation is observed between the A648 site of the α-helix HII-E-cad and the C-terminus of the α-helix H3-β-cat, which are linked by the Y654-β-cat-D665-E-cad (Y654-D665) interacting site, of 1.25 ± 0.6 nm (45% strain).
evidence: Directly stated as a simulation result with quantitative measurements.

claim: At 6 nm of extension mimicking an actual strain of 6 pN, a discrete opening of the Y654-D665 interacting site of 0.42 ± 0.08 nm occurred in 3 simulations out of 20 (15% of cases).
source: This change led, at 6 nm of extension mimicking an actual strain of 6 pN, to a discrete opening of the Y654-D665 interacting site of 0.42 ± 0.08 nm in 3 simulations out of 20, namely in 15% of cases (Figure 1b,c,d, Videos 1 and 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,b,c,d, respectively; See Figure 1c,d and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Directly stated as a simulation result with quantitative measurements and supporting figures.

claim: FLIM measurements were performed during two developmental stages: just before mesoderm invagination (late embryonic stage 5) and during invagination (stage 6).
source: FLIM measurements were performed during the two following different developmental stages during gastrulation: just before mesoderm invagination (last 10 min of cellularization, late embryonic stage 5), and during invagination (stage 6) (Figure 2b) when the acto-myosin contractile mechanical forces acting along the AJ increase in the mesoderm (Martin et al., 2010).
evidence: Directly stated as the experimental design with citation.

claim: At stage 6, measurements showed an increase of the GFP lifetime in the mesoderm of 0.073 ± 0.029 ns compared to the ectoderm, and of 0.094 ± 0.059 ns compared to stage 5 mesoderm (2.473 ns).
source: At stage 6, measurements showed an increase of the GFP lifetime in the mesoderm, observed by an increase of bright green and of yellow spots in junctions of the invaginating mesoderm (e.g. yellow arrows in Figure 2b), of 0.073 ± 0.029 ns compared to the ectoderm, and of 0.094 ± 0.059 ns compared to stage 5 mesoderm (2.473 ns) (Figure 2c, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Directly stated as experimental results with quantitative measurements.

claim: No change in the GFP donor lifetime was observed during gastrulation in the absence of injected antibody acceptor.
source: As a control, no change in the GFP donor lifetime was observed during gastrulation in the absence of injected antibody acceptor (E-cad Alexa 555 labelled AB), as well as in embryos injected with PBS alone in the absence of the antibody acceptor (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a,b and Figure 2c-right).
evidence: Directly stated as a control experiment result.

claim: The fine increase in lifetime is quantitatively in line with a mean increase in distance on the order of ~1 nm between the GFP tagged β-catenin and the fluorescently tagged E-cadherin antibody.
source: Such a fine increase in lifetime is quantitatively in line with a mean increase in distance on the order of ~1 nm (see 'Calculation of the strain from FRET efficiency variations' in the Materials and methods section) between the GFP tagged β-cat and the fluorescently tagged E-cad antibody.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the experimental results with reference to methods.

claim: The ~1 nm stretching is quantitatively predicted by the MD simulations.
source: Indeed, such ~1 nm stretching is quantitatively predicted by the MD simulations (Figure 1c).
evidence: Stated as agreement between simulation and experimental results.

claim: The lifetime increase observed specifically in the mesoderm at gastrulation shows the existence of a mechanical stretching strain between the fluorescently labelled linear domain II of E-cadherin and the C-terminus of β-catenin in the invaginating mesoderm.
source: The lifetime increase observed specifically in the mesoderm at gastrulation thus shows the existence of a mechanical stretching strain between the fluorescently labelled linear domain II of E-cad, and the C-terminus of β-cat, respectively, in the invaginating mesoderm.
evidence: Stated as the interpretation and conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: The lifetime of controls with GFP alone in the embryo junctions and with PBS injection without antibody was 2.60 ± 0.04 ns.
source: Note that the lifetime of the controls with GFP alone in the embryo junctions and with PBS injection without antibody, of 2.60 ± 0.04 ns, (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a,b, Figure 2—source data 2 and Figure 2—source data 1), was consistently higher than in the presence of the acceptor before stretching, of 2.473 ± 0.074 ns (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Directly stated as control measurements.

claim: The lifetime values are similar to the lifetime of GFP tagged proteins measured in cellula, namely 2.6 ns coupled to Histones in the nucleus in the absence of acceptor and 2.4 ns in the presence of an acceptor.
source: These values are similar to the lifetime of GFP tagged proteins measured in cellula, namely of 2.6 ns coupled to Histones in the nucleus in the absence of acceptor and of 2.4 ns in the presence of an acceptor (Llères et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated with citation to prior work for comparison.

claim: Snail and Twist were knocked-down by injecting sna and twi siRNAs for RNAi.
source: Snail and Twist were knocked-down by injecting sna and twi siRNAs for RNAi (Mitrossilis et al., 2017).
evidence: Directly stated as an experimental method with citation.

claim: Mechanical strains lacking in sna twi RNAi mesoderm invagination defective embryos were rescued by injecting ultramagnetic liposomes (UMLs) into mesoderm cells and applying a magnetic field gradient.
source: We then rescued the mechanical strains that are lacking in the sna twi RNAi mesoderm invagination defective embryos. This was achieved by injecting ultramagnetic liposomes (UMLs) into mesoderm cells (Brunet et al., 2013; Mitrossilis et al., 2017) and applying a magnetic field gradient tangential to the mesoderm, and perpendicular to its antero-posterior axis (Figure 3a and Method section).
evidence: Directly stated as an experimental method with citations.

claim: The magnetic field gradient resulted in a force that constricts cells laterally, with a deformation of the apexes similar to the uniaxial apical constriction generating mesoderm invagination.
source: This gradient resulted in a force that constricts cells laterally, with a deformation of the apexes which is similar to the uniaxial apical constriction generating mesoderm invagination (Figure 3b,c) (Sweeton et al., 1991).
evidence: Stated as the result of the magnetic manipulation with citation.

claim: No significant increase in the FRET lifetime between stage 6 and stage 5 was found in sna twi RNAi embryos defective in mesoderm invagination.
source: We found no significant increase in the FRET lifetime between stage 6 (stage of invagination in the WT) and stage 5 in sna twi RNAi embryos defective in mesoderm invagination (Figure 3d, Figure 3—source data 1, without magnet injected with UMLs and siRNAi against twi and sna), in contrast to the increase observed in the WT (Figure 2c).
evidence: Directly stated as experimental results comparing mutant to wild-type.

claim: In response to magnetically induced constriction, junctional FRET live imaging showed an increase of the lifetime of 0.098 ± 0.057 ns, comparable to the increase of 0.094 ± 0.059 ns observed in the mesoderm during its invagination.
source: In response to the magnetically induced constriction, junctional FRET live imaging showed an increase of the lifetime, observed by an increase of bright green and of yellow spots in junctions of the deformed tissue (e.g. yellow arrows in Figure 3b), of 0.098 ± 0.057 ns, comparable to the increase of 0.094 ± 0.059 ns observed in the mesoderm during its invagination.
evidence: Directly stated as experimental results with quantitative measurements.

claim: No increase in the lifetime between stage 5 and stage 6 was observed after injection of the UMLs and RNAi without magnet.
source: As controls, no increase in the lifetime between stage 5 and stage 6 was observed after injection of the UMLs and RNAi without magnet (Figure 3d), or with magnets after UML and PBS injection without the E-cad Alexa 555 acceptor (Figure 3d).
evidence: Directly stated as control experiment results.

claim: The defect of molecular mechanical strain deformation between the fluorescently labelled linear domain II of E-cadherin and the C-terminus of β-catenin in sna twi RNAi embryos is rescued mechanically.
source: Thus, the defect of molecular mechanical strain deformation between the fluorescently labelled linear domain II of E-cad and the C-terminus of β-cat in sna twi RNAi embryos is rescued mechanically.
evidence: Stated as the conclusion from the magnetic rescue experiments.

claim: The mechanical strains developed by mesoderm invagination induce a mechanical stretching deformation in the order of ~1 nm in the molecular hetero-complex between the HII-E-cadherin and H3-β-catenin helices.
source: These observations demonstrate that the mechanical strains developed by mesoderm invagination induce a mechanical stretching deformation in the order of ~1 nm in the molecular hetero-complex between the HII-E-cad and H3-β-cat helices, which are linked by the Y654-D665 site.
evidence: Stated as the conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: The experimental results confirm quantitatively the 1.25 ± 0.6 nm deformation predicted in the MD simulations.
source: These results confirm quantitatively the 1.25 ± 0.6 nm deformation predicted in our MD simulations.
evidence: Stated as agreement between simulation predictions and experimental results.

claim: An increase in the signal for the un-phosphorylated site of β-catenin at adherens junctions relative to the junctional β-catenin signal was found during gastrulation in the invaginating tissue, specific to early stage 6 and late-stage 6 compared to pre-gastrulation stage 5, of 19.6 ± 6.2% and 23.0 ± 5.7% respectively.
source: We found an increase in the signal for the un-phosphorylated site of β-cat at AJ relative to the junctional β-cat signal during gastrulation in the invaginating tissue. The increase is specific of gastrulation early stage 6 and late-stage 6 compared to pre-gastrulation stage 5, of 19.6 ± 6.2% and 23.0 ± 5.7% respectively (Figure 4a,c, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Directly stated as experimental results with quantitative measurements.

claim: No increase in the signal for the un-phosphorylated site of β-catenin at adherens junctions relative to the junctional β-catenin signal was observed in the ectoderm, which is less strained.
source: As a control, no increase in the signal for the un-phosphorylated site of β-cat at AJ relative to the junctional β-cat signal observed in the ectoderm, which is less strained (Figure 4d, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Directly stated as control experiment results.

claim: Under the molecular strain induced by the morphogenetic movement of invagination, the Y654 site increases its accessibility by nearly 20 ± 5% to specific molecular interactions before being phosphorylated.
source: This result thus shows that under the molecular strain induced by the morphogenetic movement of invagination, the Y654 site increases its accessibility by nearly 20 ± 5% to specific molecular interactions, before being phosphorylated.
evidence: Stated as the interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: In the src42A RNAi knockdown background, a specific increase in the signal for the un-phosphorylated site of β-catenin at adherens junctions under strain was found, measured relative to the junctional β-catenin signal during gastrulation (44.3 ± 7.3% and 45.1 ± 7.9%, respectively), and of about 25 ± 5% compared to wild type, both at early stage 6 and late-stage 6.
source: In the src42A RNAi knockdown background, we found a specific increase in the signal for the un-phosphorylated site of β-cat at AJ under strain, as observed by the increase of Y654-βcat green labelling that adds to, and dominates the β-cat red labelling, leading to a bright green/yellow composite colour (Figure 4b). This signal was measured relative to the junctional β-cat signal during gastrulation (44.3 ± 7.3% and 45.1 ± 7.9%, respectively), and of about 25 ± 5% compared to wild type, both at early stage 6 and late-stage 6 (Figure 4b,c).
evidence: Directly stated as experimental results with quantitative measurements.

claim: No significant increase in the signal for the un-phosphorylated site of β-catenin at adherens junctions relative to the junctional β-catenin signal was observed in the ectoderm in the src42A RNAi embryos compared to the wild type.
source: As a control, no significant increase in the signal for the un-phosphorylated site of β-cat at AJ relative to the junctional β-cat signal is observed in the ectoderm, that is less strained, in the src42A RNAi embryos compared to the WT (Figure 4d).
evidence: Directly stated as control experiment results.

claim: An increase of 12.4 ± 5.8% and 9.3 ± 4.3% respectively was observed in the signal for the un-phosphorylated site of β-catenin at adherens junctions in the mesoderm normalized to the un-phosphorylated site of β-catenin ectoderm, in the src42A RNAi embryos compared to the wild type.
source: Consistently, an increase of 12.4 ± 5.8% and 9.3 ± 4.3% respectively, is observed in the signal for the un-phosphorylated site of site of β-cat at AJ in the mesoderm normalized to the un-phosphorylated site of β-cat ectoderm, in the src42A RNAi embryos compared to the WT (Figure 4e).
evidence: Directly stated as experimental results with quantitative measurements.

claim: During mesoderm invagination, the accessibility of the Y654 β-catenin site to Src42A increases due to its mechanical opening.
source: Therefore, we conclude that during mesoderm invagination, the accessibility of the site of Y654 β-cat to Src42A increases due to its mechanical opening.
evidence: Stated as the conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: The Y654 β-catenin residue becomes specifically more available for Src42A phosphorylation at adherens junctions as the strain builds up at the Y654 β-catenin-D665 E-cadherin molecular complex interaction site.
source: At the same time, the Y654 β-cat residue becomes specifically more available for Src42A phosphorylation at AJ, as the strain builds up at the Y654 β-cat-D665-E-cad molecular complex interaction site.
evidence: Stated as the conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: Upon photobleaching, the fluorescent recovery amplitude (mobile fraction) of β-catenin is increased by 16 ± 6% when mesoderm invagination has built up at mid-stage 6.
source: We found upon photobleaching that the fluorescent recovery amplitude, the so-called mobile fraction, of β-cat upon photobleaching is increased by 16 ± 6% when mesoderm invagination has built up at mid-stage 6.
evidence: Directly stated as experimental results with quantitative measurements.

claim: The increase in mobile fraction indicates that about 16% more molecules at the adherens junctions are able to be recycled and exchanged at stage 6 compared to stage 5.
source: This observation indicated that about 16% more molecules at the AJ are able to be recycled and exchanged at stage 6 compared to stage 5 (Figure 5c,d, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Stated as the interpretation of the FRAP experimental results.

claim: The FRAP result is consistent with studies examining β-catenin turnover at cellular junctions under strain during germ band extension.
source: This result is consistent with studies examining β-cat turnover at cellular junctions under strain during germ band extension (Tamada et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated with citation to prior work for comparison.

claim: The 16% increase in mobile fraction is quantitatively predicted by the 15% probability of opening the β-catenin/E-cadherin complex observed in the MD simulations under strain.
source: This effect is quantitatively predicted by the 15% probability of opening the β-cat/E-cad complex observed in our MD simulations under strain.
evidence: Stated as agreement between simulation predictions and experimental results.

claim: The opening of the Y654-D665 interacting site leads to increased Src42A phosphorylation, which leads to decreased affinity between β-catenin and E-cadherin.
source: As the opening of the Y654-D665 interacting site will lead to an increased Src42A phosphorylation, it will therefore lead to a decreased affinity between β-cat and E-cad.
evidence: Stated as a logical inference from the experimental results.

claim: The morphogenetic movements of invagination locally cause a mechanical stretch at the Y654-D665 interaction site in the β-catenin/E-cadherin molecular complex.
source: This relationship shows that the morphogenetic movements of invagination locally cause a mechanical stretch at the Y654-D665 interaction site in the β-cat/E-cad molecular complex.
evidence: Stated as the conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: The mechanical stretch statistically weakens the interaction of β-catenin with E-cadherin in adherens junctions of the mesoderm cells and thereby favours cytosolic β-catenin enrichment.
source: It indeed statistically weakens the interaction of β-cat with E-cad in AJ of the mesoderm cells and thereby favours cytosolic β-cat enrichment.
evidence: Stated as the conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: In the gastrulating Drosophila embryo, the Src42A kinase required for the mechanical induction of Y654-β-catenin phosphorylation is already activated (phosphorylated on Y400) before tissue deformation.
source: In the gastrulating Drosophila embryo, the Src42A kinase required for the mechanical induction of Y654-β−cat phosphorylation is already activated (phosphorylated on Y400) before tissue deformation.
evidence: Stated as a known fact about the system.

claim: Src42A is not mechanically 'over-activated' by tissue deformation during the morphogenetic movements of gastrulation.
source: Therefore, Src42A is surprisingly not mechanically 'over-activated' by tissue deformation during the morphogenetic movements of gastrulation (Desprat et al., 2008), and is thus not upstream of the mechanotransduction pathway leading to Y654-β-cat phosphorylation.
evidence: Stated with citation to prior work.

claim: The already activated form of Src42A is permissively required in the mechanotransductive process leading to the activation of β-catenin release from the junctions into the cytoplasm and then to the nucleus.
source: In contrast, the already activated form of Src42A is permissively required in the mechanotransductive process leading to the activation of β-cat release from the junctions into the cytoplasm and then to the nucleus.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the mechanotransduction mechanism.

claim: The highly evolutionary conserved Y654 β-catenin-D665-E-cadherin major interaction site of the adherens junction complex acts as primary mechanosensor.
source: Here we showed that the highly evolutionary conserved Y654 β-cat-D665-E-cad major interaction site of the AJ complex acts as primary mechanosensor.
evidence: Stated as the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The Y654 β-catenin-D665-E-cadherin site activates the β-catenin pathway through its mechanical opening in vivo that enables phosphorylation by Src42A kinase.
source: The site activates the β-cat pathway through its mechanical opening in vivo that enables phosphorylation by Src42A kinase.
evidence: Stated as the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Phosphorylation leads to the decrease of the Y654 β-catenin-D665-E-cadherin affinity and to the release of β-catenin into the cytosol.
source: Phosphorylation in turn leads to the decrease of the Y654 β-cat-D665-E-cad affinity (Roura et al., 1999; van Veelen et al., 2011), and to the release of β-cat into the cytosol.
evidence: Stated with citations to prior work.

claim: The release of β-catenin leads to target developmental patterning gene transcription in the nucleus.
source: This release finally leads to target developmental patterning gene transcription in the nucleus (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) (Brunet et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated with citation to prior work.

claim: The study demonstrates in vivo the existence of a primary molecular mechano-chemical translator functionally involved in the trans-scale activation of a molecular physiological differentiation pathway in response to an endogenously produced macroscopic mechanical strain.
source: We thereby demonstrate in vivo the existence of a primary molecular mechano-chemical translator. It is functionally involved in the trans-scale activation of a molecular physiological differentiation pathway, in response to an endogenously produced macroscopic mechanical strain.
evidence: Stated as the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The mechanosensor is the Y654-β-catenin/D665-E-cadherin interaction site of the hetero β-catenin/E-cadherin complex at adherens junctions.
source: Here, the mechanosensor is the Y654-β-cat/D665-E-cad interaction site of the hetero β-cat/E-cad complex at AJ.
evidence: Stated as the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The mechanosensor opens under strain and favours the phosphorylation of β-catenin by Src42A.
source: It opens under strain and favours the phosphorylation of β-cat by Src42A.
evidence: Stated as the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The mechanical activation of the β-catenin pathway initiates early mesoderm differentiation and specification in response to the strain associated to mesoderm invagination at the onset of Drosophila's embryonic gastrulation.
source: This process initiates early mesoderm differentiation and specification in response to the strain associated to mesoderm invagination at the onset of Drosophila's embryonic gastrulation.
evidence: Stated as the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The soft stretching of 1 nm between the two α-helices surrounding the Y654-β-catenin/D665 E-cadherin major interaction site leads to a probability of 15% opening and release of signalling β-catenin from the junctions after phosphorylation by Src42A.
source: The soft stretching of 1 nm between the two α--helices surrounding the Y654-β-cat/D665 E-cad major interaction site leads to a probability of 15% opening and release of signalling β-cat from the junctions after phosphorylation by Src42A.
evidence: Stated as the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Low levels of β-catenin are sufficient to trigger transcription into the nucleus.
source: Such finely tuned process could trigger the mechanotransductive signalling translocation from AJ to the nucleus of low levels of β-cat, known to be sufficient to trigger transcription into the nucleus (Peifer and Wieschaus, 1990), and ensure the maintenance of tissue coherence by the maintenance of 85% of the β-cat in the junctions.
evidence: Stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Both the Y654-β-catenin and D665 E-cadherin major sites between the two molecules are strongly conserved across all metazoa.
source: Finally, both the Y654-β-cat and D665 E-cad major sites between the two molecules are strongly conserved across all metazoa (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Stated with reference to sequence alignment figure.

claim: This mechanotransductive molecular sensor may be generic in the overall animal kingdom and be involved in physiological mechanical induction processes, including mesoderm differentiation across all bilaterians.
source: This mechanotransductive molecular sensor may thus be generic in the overall animal kingdom, and be involved in physiological mechanical induction processes, including mesoderm differentiation across all bilaterians (Brunet et al., 2013), and pathological processes, including mechanical induction of tumour differentiation in response to tumour growth pressure in most epithelia of most animals (Fernández-Sánchez et al., 2015b).
evidence: Stated as speculation about broader implications with citations.

claim: The mechanotransductive molecular sensor may be involved in pathological processes, including mechanical induction of tumour differentiation in response to tumour growth pressure in most epithelia of most animals.
source: This mechanotransductive molecular sensor may thus be generic in the overall animal kingdom, and be involved in physiological mechanical induction processes, including mesoderm differentiation across all bilaterians (Brunet et al., 2013), and pathological processes, including mechanical induction of tumour differentiation in response to tumour growth pressure in most epithelia of most animals (Fernández-Sánchez et al., 2015b).
evidence: Stated as speculation about broader implications with citations.

claim: Mechanical stresses are inherent to multi-cellular tissues in organisms and can regulate signalling pathways involved in biochemical patterning and biomechanical morphogenesis.
source: Mechanical stresses are inherent to multi-cellular tissues in organisms, and can regulate signalling pathways involved both in their biochemical patterning and biomechanical morphogenesis (Brouzés and Farge, 2004; Chan et al., 2017; Mammoto and Ingber, 2010; Wozniak and Chen, 2009).
evidence: Stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Mechanical regulation is involved in physiological developmental processes and pathological processes such as tumorigenesis.
source: Mechanical regulation is involved not only in physiological developmental processes, but also in pathological processes such as in tumorigenesis (Mitrossilis et al., 2017; Dupont et al., 2011; Baeyens et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2015; Engler et al., 2006; Vogel and Sheetz, 2009; McBeath et al., 2004; Paszek et al., 2014; Uyttewaal et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2011; Farge, 2003).
evidence: Stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Mechanotransduction consists in the translation of mechanical strains submitted to living cells into biochemical signals.
source: Such regulation is based on molecular mechanotransductional processes, which consist in the translation of mechanical strains submitted to living cells into biochemical signals (Gospodarowicz et al., 1978; Nakache and Gaub, 1988; Kanno et al., 2007; Bissell et al., 2005; Rubashkin et al., 2014; Delarue et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2015; Mammoto et al., 2009; Yan et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated with citations to prior work.

claim: The molecular basis of mechanotransduction is the activation or modulation of biochemical reactions in response to cell or tissue mechanical strain-deformations.
source: The molecular basis of mechanotransduction is the activation or modulation of biochemical reactions in response to cell or tissue mechanical strain-deformations.
evidence: Stated as a general principle.

claim: Free-energy barriers between protein conformations are usually smaller than a few tens of kT.
source: Since free-energy barriers between protein conformations are usually smaller than a few tens of kT (Lannon et al., 2012) (i.e several ten times the molecular thermal energy), mechanical stresses applied to biomolecular structures can a priori easily trigger conformational changes.
evidence: Stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Mechanical stresses applied to biomolecular structures can easily trigger conformational changes.
source: Since free-energy barriers between protein conformations are usually smaller than a few tens of kT (Lannon et al., 2012) (i.e several ten times the molecular thermal energy), mechanical stresses applied to biomolecular structures can a priori easily trigger conformational changes.
evidence: Stated as an inference from the energy barrier information.

claim: Mechanical deformations can lead to changes in molecular biochemical reactivity and states, thereby initiating the activation or modulation of biochemical signal-transduction pathways.
source: Such deformations can subsequently lead to changes in the molecular biochemical reactivity and states, thereby initiating the activation or modulation of biochemical signal-transduction pathways (Brujic et al., 2007; Fernandez-Sanchez et al., 2015a; Grashoff et al., 2010; Vargas et al., 2001).
evidence: Stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Mechanical stresses have been shown to initiate a variety of molecular protein-conformation or membrane shape changes in cell culture.
source: Mechanical stresses have been shown to initiate a variety of molecular protein-conformation, or membrane shape changes, in cell culture.
evidence: Stated as a general observation from prior work.

claim: Mechanical stress renders accessible the phosphorylation target site for Src-kinase in the p130Cas protein involved in tumorigenic cell migration.
source: One example is the rendering of accessibility of the phosphorylation target site for kinases, like for Src-kinase, in the p130Cas protein involved in tumorigenic cell migration, in response to mechanical stress (Sawada et al., 2006).
evidence: Stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Mechanically induced inhibition of the formation of endocytic vesicles leads to the inhibition or degradation of interactions of secreted ligand-receptor complexes and activates or enhances downstream signalling pathways.
source: Another example is the mechanically induced inhibition of the formation of endocytic vesicles that lead to the inhibition or the degradation of interactions of secreted ligand-receptor complexes and thus activate or enhance downstream signalling pathways.
evidence: Stated as a general mechanism.

claim: Mechanically induced inhibition of endocytic vesicle formation was shown in cell culture for BMP2 inducing myoblast/osteoblast trans-differentiation.
source: This was shown in cell culture for BMP2 inducing myoblast/osteoblast trans-differentiation (Rauch et al., 2002).
evidence: Stated with citation to prior work.

claim: None of the underlying molecular mechanisms of mechanotransduction characterized so far has been found to be functionally involved in cell specification and differentiation in vivo.
source: However, none of the underlying molecular mechanism of mechanotransduction characterized so far has been found to be functionally involved in cell specification and differentiation, in vivo.
evidence: Stated as a gap in knowledge that this study addresses.

claim: The β-catenin pathway is mechanotransductively involved in major biochemical patterning processes in both developmental and tumorous contexts.
source: Among the many mechanosensitive pathways, the β-catenin (β-cat) pathway is mechanotransductively involved in major biochemical patterning processes in both developmental and tumorous contexts (Fernandez-Sanchez et al., 2015a; Farge, 2003; Desprat et al., 2008; Brunet et al., 2013; Benham-Pyle et al., 2015; Fernández-Sánchez et al., 2015b; Samuel et al., 2011; Whitehead et al., 2008; Mouw et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Mechanical activation of β-catenin and downstream transcriptional signaling is vitally involved in embryonic anterior endoderm specification in response to the first morphogenetic movements of gastrulation.
source: Initially, it was found that mechanical activation of β-cat and downstream transcriptional signaling is vitally involved in embryonic anterior endoderm specification in response to the first morphogenetic movements of gastrulation (Farge, 2003; Desprat et al., 2008)
evidence: Stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Mechanical activation of β-catenin is involved in ex-vivo reconstructed epithelial cells in response to mechanical stretching.
source: In addition, it is involved in ex-vivo reconstructed epithelial cells in response to mechanical stretching (Benham-Pyle et al., 2015; Benham-Pyle et al., 2016), in tumor progression in healthy tissues in response to neighboring tumor growth pressure and stiffness (Fernández-Sánchez et al., 2015b; Samuel et al., 2011; Whitehead et al., 2008), or in follicle development initiation (Shyer et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Mechanical activation of β-catenin is involved in tumor progression in healthy tissues in response to neighboring tumor growth pressure and stiffness.
source: In addition, it is involved in ex-vivo reconstructed epithelial cells in response to mechanical stretching (Benham-Pyle et al., 2015; Benham-Pyle et al., 2016), in tumor progression in healthy tissues in response to neighboring tumor growth pressure and stiffness (Fernández-Sánchez et al., 2015b; Samuel et al., 2011; Whitehead et al., 2008), or in follicle development initiation (Shyer et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Mechanical activation of β-catenin is involved in follicle development initiation.
source: In addition, it is involved in ex-vivo reconstructed epithelial cells in response to mechanical stretching (Benham-Pyle et al., 2015; Benham-Pyle et al., 2016), in tumor progression in healthy tissues in response to neighboring tumor growth pressure and stiffness (Fernández-Sánchez et al., 2015b; Samuel et al., 2011; Whitehead et al., 2008), or in follicle development initiation (Shyer et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated with citations to prior work.

claim: In both zebrafish and Drosophila embryos, early mesoderm differentiation was found to be mechanically induced by the very first morphogenetic movements of embryogenesis through the mechanical activation of the β-catenin pathway.
source: In both zebrafish and Drosophila embryos, early mesoderm differentiation was also found to be mechanically induced by the very first morphogenetic movements of embryogenesis. This induction occurs through the mechanical activation of the β-cat pathway, where the mechanical strain generated by the onset of embryonic morphogenesis mechanically induces the Src-family kinase (SFK) dependent phosphorylation of the highly conserved β-cat Y654 site (Brunet et al., 2013; Fernández-Sánchez et al., 2015b), a major site of interaction with E-cadherin (E-cad) in adherens junctions (AJ) (Roura et al., 1999; van Veelen et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated with citations to prior work.

claim: The mechanical strain generated by the onset of embryonic morphogenesis mechanically induces the Src-family kinase dependent phosphorylation of the highly conserved β-catenin Y654 site.
source: This induction occurs through the mechanical activation of the β-cat pathway, where the mechanical strain generated by the onset of embryonic morphogenesis mechanically induces the Src-family kinase (SFK) dependent phosphorylation of the highly conserved β-cat Y654 site (Brunet et al., 2013; Fernández-Sánchez et al., 2015b), a major site of interaction with E-cadherin (E-cad) in adherens junctions (AJ) (Roura et al., 1999; van Veelen et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated with citations to prior work.

claim: The Y654 site is a major site of interaction with E-cadherin in adherens junctions.
source: This induction occurs through the mechanical activation of the β-cat pathway, where the mechanical strain generated by the onset of embryonic morphogenesis mechanically induces the Src-family kinase (SFK) dependent phosphorylation of the highly conserved β-cat Y654 site (Brunet et al., 2013; Fernández-Sánchez et al., 2015b), a major site of interaction with E-cadherin (E-cad) in adherens junctions (AJ) (Roura et al., 1999; van Veelen et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Phosphorylation of the Y654 site leads to β-catenin release from adherens junctions and its translocation to the nucleus, where it activates the transcription of early mesodermal key specification genes.
source: This chemical modification leads to β-cat release from AJ and its translocation to the nucleus, where it activates the transcription of early mesodermal key specification genes (Brunet et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated with citation to prior work.

claim: The molecular mechanism of mechanotransduction that mechanically initiates Src-family kinase-dependent β-catenin phosphorylation in vivo, as well as its primary mechano-sensor, are still unknown.
source: The molecular mechanism of mechanotransduction that mechanically initiates such SFK-dependent β-cat phosphorylation in vivo, as well as its primary mechano-sensor, are still unknown.
evidence: Stated as a gap in knowledge that this study addresses.
